title: Americans judge the press-government relationship as bad while disagreeing over media power and permissible criticism
source_unit: Pew Research Center Pew-Knight Initiative surveys and focus groups on press freedom

observations.period: June 22-28, 2026; perceived relationship between the Trump administration and US news media

denominator.unit: percent of US adults in Pew survey; respondents who did not answer are not shown

bad_relationship.unit: percent saying the relationship is very or somewhat bad

good_relationship.unit: percent saying the relationship is very or somewhat good

neutral_relationship.unit: percent saying the relationship is neutral

observations.method: Pew Research Center American Trends Panel survey; current 2026 result compared in the source with 2025, plus ten online focus groups used for illustrative qualitative context.
observations.uncertainty: The relationship judgment is a perception, not an independently coded measure of press freedom, censorship, institutional conduct, or news accuracy. Focus groups are illustrative and not representative of US adults.
observations.subgroup: US adults; the source reports age, news-following, press-freedom-importance, and partisan comparisons separately.
observations.counterinterpretation: People can agree that the relationship is bad while assigning responsibility to different actors or approving of the conflict; shared diagnosis does not imply shared legitimacy judgment.

observations.period: June 22-28, 2026; perceived political power of US news organizations

denominator.unit: percent of US adults in Pew survey; respondents who did not answer are not shown

too_much_power_overall.unit: percent saying news organizations have too much power and influence in politics

too_much_power_republican.unit: percent among Republicans and Republican leaners

too_much_power_democratic.unit: percent among Democrats and Democratic leaners

partisan_contrast.unit: percentage-point contrast, Republican/lean Republican minus Democratic/lean Democratic

observations.method: Pew partisan comparison of perceived news-organization power in politics; party groups include independents who lean toward each party as defined by the source.
observations.uncertainty: Perceived power is not a measure of audience reach, ownership concentration, agenda-setting effect, or actual institutional influence. The partisan contrast is descriptive and may reflect political identity, media use, and incumbent/opposition position.
observations.subgroup: US adults overall and party-identification groups.
observations.counterinterpretation: A respondent can view news organizations as powerful yet support press criticism, distrust particular outlets, or want more rather than less scrutiny; the item is not a single trust score.

observations.period: June 22-28, 2026; acceptability of public criticism between journalists and politicians

denominator.unit: percent of US adults in Pew survey; respondents who did not answer are not shown

journalists_criticizing_politicians_acce.unit: percent saying completely or somewhat acceptable

politicians_criticizing_journalists_acce.unit: percent saying completely or somewhat acceptable

directional_contrast.unit: percentage-point contrast favoring acceptability of journalist criticism of politicians

observations.method: Pew survey item on normative acceptability; the source also reports party and press-freedom-importance conditioning.
observations.uncertainty: Acceptability is a normative attitude, not observed speech, harassment, retaliation, censorship, editorial independence, or legal constraint. The two directions may invoke different standards for accountability and power.
observations.subgroup: US adults overall; party and press-freedom-importance subgroups are reported by Pew.
observations.counterinterpretation: A majority approval of criticism in either direction does not establish support for every tactic, tone, or institutional consequence, and it does not imply willingness to act politically.

related_sources.claim: Pew's companion key-findings page defines the press-freedom study and its survey/focus-group design.
Prior Pew news/government results provide historical context for the relationship measure.

boundary: This record measures perceptions and norms concerning press-government relations, media power, and reciprocal criticism. It does not measure actual censorship, news accuracy, ownership, audience exposure, institutional trust as a general construct, political participation, vote choice, or causal media effects. The focus groups are not representative and are not pooled with survey estimates.
